references.text: Aaron had previously allowed the people to run wild by building the golden calf, which led to the condition Moses now observes.
Describes how the people quickly turned away from the Lord's way, resulting in them becoming 'unrestrained' or out of control.
The Hebrew word 'פָּרַע' (para) is also used here in connection with letting down the hair, indicating a lack of control or order.
Proverbs warns that without prophetic vision, the people become unrestrained (פָּרַע), from the same root as in Exodus 32:25.
Israel was made a shame among their enemies because of sin, paralleling how the people's behavior led to 'shame among their enemies'.
Stephen refers to this event in his speech and describes how the Israelites turned away and rejoiced in the work of their own hands.
Paul warns believers against idolatry by pointing to the golden calf incident as a cautionary example.
Connects Aaron's failed leadership regarding the golden calf with his later role as an intercessor to stop God's wrath.
Creates a theological contrast between the people's fear of God's glory (Moses) and their lack of fear in sin (Aaron).
Contrasts Aaron's failed leadership concerning the golden calf with his successful efforts at the dedication of the tabernacle.
Highlights the theme of the people's resistance to and abandonment of God's chosen leaders (Moses and Aaron) in various contexts.
Direct narrative connection: Verse 5 describes the origin of the unrestrained behavior that verse 25 concludes with.
Contrasts Aaron's faithful role as God's speaker in the wilderness with his failure as a leader at the golden calf.
